newsitem.title: USA: Tele-Communications CEO says bad days over.
newsitem.headline: Tele-Communications CEO says bad days over.

text.p: Armed with figures showing better operating cash flow, a key barometer in the cable TV industry, Tele-Communications Inc. Chief Executive John Malone said on Wednesday the company's recent bad times were behind it.

"Our core cable business is now restored to its vitality, has clear operating plans in place ... and a strong financial base by which to do it," Malone told reporters after the company's annual investors' meeting.
Preliminary figures on cash flow, released late Tuesday, were the kind of news the Englewood, Colorado based company wanted to report during the important meeting with investors.

Operating cash flow rose 23.7 percent to $704 million in the first quarter over the year-earlier period. Securities analysts were looking for a lower figure of between $640 and $675 million. Final results will be released in a few weeks.
Malone also said projects to offer telephone service to customers will be delayed "because of regulatory and economic issues."
Malone said TCI will focus on developing high-speed data services.
TCI stock has been in the doldrums and in December the company announced layoffs of about 2,500 people. Other cost cutting measures were implemented.

At the annual conference lenders wanted to know if the first quarter performance was sustainable while investors want to know if the company can keep its promises, said Leo Hindery, TCI's new president.
"I hope they believed me," Hindery told Reuters. "I've never promised anything I didn't perform," Hindery added.

But while the operating cash flow numbers were impressive the picture was not all rosy. In the first three months of the year TCI lost about 83,000 basic customers, bringing its total customer base to about 14.3 million.
One investor who attended the meeting and declined to be identified, said the big worry was TCI's customer relations.
Hindery, who was brought in recently by Malone, could not agree more, calling relations with customers "pitiful."
Hindery vowed that the next time the company implements a rate hike, he will add channels at the same time, so customers do not feel cheated.
Some of the recent customer loss was attributed to rate hikes earlier this year. Hindery said "the bleeding stopped in the second week of March" and customer numbers rose in April.
But because cable customer numbers tend to drop in the summer, Hindery told the press briefing that he does not foresee increases until later this year.
But what TCI is banking on is collecting more customer dollars by offering a better product.
By the end of the year, TCI will be offering to most of its customers a new digital television product with more channels and Internet access.

No corporate figures exist for how many customers will sign on, but Hindery said his "feeling" is that about 30 percent will want the new offering and be willng to pay about $10 a month for it, bringing their average monthly cable bill to about $35.
Hindery said such a goal could be accomplished in "two to 2-1/2 years."
A good deal of TCI's higher costs are attributed to its programming costs, the channel offerings on its cable systems.
